claims.text: An integrated machine-learning-guided processing framework can identify a unified thermo-mechanical treatment.
The identified treatment can simultaneously enhance phase stability, refine microstructure, and improve properties in multiphase metallic systems.
The target material has coexisting phases and suboptimal grain sizes in its conventional polycrystalline state.
A closed-loop data-driven approach can correlate deformation strain, temperature profiles, and annealing times with phase formation, grain refinement, and material properties.
The proposed processing regime combines controlled mechanical deformation with tailored thermal exposure.
High-energy milling and sintering-like treatments provide relevant reproducible thermo-mechanical conditions for the proposed framework.
Balanced thermal and deformation inputs induce optimized phase-boundary characteristics.
Balanced thermal and deformation inputs induce a refined grain structure.
Mining historical process-structure-property datasets allows a machine-learning model to predict synergistic processing parameters.
The predicted processing parameters can stabilize desired phases while simultaneously refining the microstructure.
Refined grain structure and controlled phase boundaries govern the optimized mechanical or functional properties.
The optimized treatment will reduce unwanted phase transformations relative to conventional sequential processing.
The optimized treatment will produce finer grains and more controlled phase boundaries than conventional sequential processing.
The optimized treatment will improve mechanical or functional properties relative to conventional sequential processing.
Conventional multi-step processing commonly improves phase stability, grain refinement, or properties sequentially and incurs trade-offs among them.
The method is most applicable to multiphase metallic systems under controlled thermo-mechanical conditions.
Extreme compositions or non-standard processing environments may cause deviations from the predicted results.
X-ray diffraction, electron microscopy, and mechanical testing can respectively assess phase behavior, grain and boundary characteristics, and mechanical properties in the proposed comparison.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in all three target categories relative to the conventional-process control would falsify the hypothesis.
